word:lxx:L706464.explanation: Iachin, also rendered Iakhin, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals in genealogical and priestly lists rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name appears six times in six Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Nehemiah. Its exact significance as a personal name is not explained by the available passages, so the clearest meaning is simply the name itself: Iachin or Iakhin.

word:lxx:L706510.explanation: Iealē, also given as Ieali, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as an identifying name in the Greek Old Testament, distinguishing someone named in the biblical record. The available information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the person or group associated with it. This name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:58.

word:lxx:L706569.explanation: Iethnouēl, also rendered Iethnoil, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not presented here as a general term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:2. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional definition or explanation of its parts. Its precise significance in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage and the person being named.

word:lxx:L706587.explanation: Iemla is a proper name, used to identify a person rather than to describe an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX), it appears four times, in four verses: twice in 1 Kings 22 and twice in 2 Chronicles 18. The name itself is given as “Iemla,” without an additional English definition. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L706675.explanation: Iescha, also rendered Ieskha, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a woman named in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 11:29. Because it is a proper name, its main function is to identify the person who bears it, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about her place in the family narrative.

word:lxx:L706752.explanation: This noun means a fowler, or bird-catcher—someone who captures birds. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Amos, and refers to the person who sets or uses a trap for birds. The word itself identifies the bird-catcher rather than the bird or the trap. Its appearances are in Amos 3:5, 8:1, and 8:2, but the precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L706846.explanation: Histēmi means to stand or establish. It describes standing in place and can also describe establishing something, such as a covenant.

word:lxx:L706891.explanation: This word is a proper personal name, rendered as “Iōannēn” or “Ioannin.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. Within the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 1 Maccabees. The listed occurrences are in 1 Maccabees 9:36, 13:53, 16:2, and 16:19. The precise person identified in each passage must be determined from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

word:lxx:L707009.explanation: This verb means “fly down,” describing movement from a higher position toward a lower one. It presents the action plainly, without by itself explaining why something descends or what happens afterward. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 43:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the downward movement of flying.

word:lxx:L707070.explanation: Kakourgos means a malefactor, or wrongdoer.

word:lxx:L707144.explanation: Karee, also rendered Karie, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in 2 Kings and Jeremiah. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide verse text or a further definition, its precise referent must be understood from the surrounding passage in each occurrence. The name appears in 2 Kings 25:23 and several passages in Jeremiah.

word:lxx:L707221.explanation: This adjective describes something so unreasonable, foolish, or laughable that it appears ridiculous or absurd. It is used to characterize a person, action, claim, or situation rather than to name an object by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 17:8. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what is being called ridiculous there, but the word’s basic sense is clear: it marks something as plainly nonsensical or worthy of ridicule.

word:lxx:L707368.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to mourn for someone or to bewail them—that is, to express deep grief over a person or loss. It describes an act of lament rather than a mere feeling of sadness. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Exodus 33:4. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is grieving openly for someone or something. word:lxx:L707566.explanation: This adjective means “burning” or “scorching,” describing something characterized by intense heat. It functions as a descriptive modifier, helping identify the heat-producing or searing quality of a thing rather than naming an object or action itself. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense is physical and heat-related, while the surrounding verse identifies what is burning or scorching.

word:lxx:L707625.explanation: This noun means “horn,” referring to the horn of an animal or to a horn-shaped object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs 95 times, from Genesis through 2 Maccabees. The word appears in descriptions involving animals, worship, kingship, and prophetic imagery, but its basic meaning remains horn. The surrounding verse determines whether the reference is literal or figurative.

word:lxx:L707698.explanation: This proper name refers to “Kitioi; Kiti.” It functions as a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Genesis 10:4 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:7. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the name’s specific reference in each passage must be understood from those genealogical contexts. Its consistent use as a proper name is the central meaning available for this LXX term.

word:lxx:L707720.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “branch,” referring to a woody shoot or limb growing from a tree or vine. It is used for parts of plants and trees, whether fresh, spreading, or capable of bearing growth. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, with several occurrences in Ezekiel and others in prophetic books. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and imagery.

word:lxx:L707759.explanation: This LXX noun means “hollow,” referring to a hollow place or feature. It functions as a naming word for such a thing, rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 8:14. The word’s basic sense is therefore concise: it identifies a hollow. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L707812.explanation: This noun means “plaster; stucco,” referring to a material used as a coating or surface covering. It names a physical building substance rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 5:5. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense remains the plaster or stucco material itself.

word:lxx:L707971.explanation: Kymbalizō means to play the cymbals.

word:lxx:L708035.explanation: Laada is a proper name, rendered “Laada” and also associated with the form “Laatha.” It functions as a personal or identifying name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:21. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity cannot be determined here, but its lexical role is simply a named designation.

word:lxx:L708088.explanation: This verb means “go unnoticed” or describe someone as “unaware.” It expresses a lack of awareness: something is not recognized, observed, or noticed, or a person does not realize what has happened. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as an action or state involving things escaping attention. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Leviticus, Numbers, Job, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence presents as unnoticed or unaware.

word:lxx:L708123.explanation: Lebōna, also rendered Levona, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This form occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Judges 21:19, so its ordinary function is identifying a particular name rather than expressing a general vocabulary meaning. The available lexical information does not establish a broader symbolic or descriptive sense.

word:lxx:L708181.explanation: Lēstēs means a bandit or robber.

word:lxx:L708347.explanation: The word means “Magus” and functions as a noun naming a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel chapter 2: Daniel 2:2 and Daniel 2:10. These references locate its uses, but the word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording. As a lexical term, it identifies the person designated by this noun.

word:lxx:L708439.explanation: This verb describes acting cowardly—showing a lack of courage rather than standing firm. It names an action marked by timidity in the face of difficulty, danger, pressure, or duty. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:17. The word itself gives the basic description; the surrounding passage is needed to identify exactly what prompted the cowardice in that verse.

word:lxx:L708440.explanation: This verb means “soften”: to make something less hard, severe, or firm. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 23:16. As a verb, it describes an action or change rather than a person, object, or quality. The word’s precise force in Job depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here; its clear lexical idea is becoming or making something softer.

word:lxx:L708541.explanation: This word is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is represented as “Masezebēl” or “Masezevil.” In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:4. Because it is a name, its ordinary meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who a person is, while the surrounding passage supplies that person’s role and significance. No additional lexical definition or contextual description is provided here.

word:lxx:L708606.explanation: Machiri, also written Makhiri, is a proper name identifying an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship; its meaning is the personal name itself. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 26:33. Without the verse text and surrounding context, the name alone does not establish additional details about the person or the role connected with him.

word:lxx:L708754.explanation: Merran is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; its role is to identify someone within the passage. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, Merran occurs once, in Baruch 3:23. The name itself supplies no further meaning beyond this personal designation, so understanding the person’s significance requires the surrounding verse and passage. Merran remains a distinct LXX name rather than a general word translated by an ordinary English term.

word:lxx:L708817.explanation: Metastrephō means to reverse or turn back.

word:lxx:L708880.explanation: Mēniō means to be wroth with or angry with someone.

word:lxx:L708978.explanation: Adultery means sexual unfaithfulness within marriage—the violation of the marriage covenant by giving sexual intimacy to someone other than one’s spouse. It is a noun naming this wrongful act. In the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish Scriptures represented here, the word appears four times, always with the meaning “adultery.” Its occurrences are found in Jeremiah, Hosea, and Wisdom, showing that the term is used across both prophetic and wisdom writings. The surrounding verse determines how the act is being addressed in each passage.

word:lxx:L709142.explanation: This word means “harp” or “stringed instrument,” referring to a musical instrument used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. As a noun, it names the instrument itself rather than the act of playing it. It occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages describing groups of musicians and musical worship. The precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L709216.explanation: Naphthō is a proper name, rendered “Naphthō” or “Naftho.” It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament, but the available information does not specify which. This name occurs twice in the Greek translation of Joshua, in Joshua 15:9 and Joshua 18:15. Its meaning is therefore primarily its role as a name rather than a descriptive word with a separate everyday definition.

word:lxx:L709263.explanation: Nestha is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 24:8. The available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, so it does not establish further details about the person or the role the name has in that verse.

word:lxx:L709348.explanation: This noun means “feeding-place,” referring to a place where nourishment is provided or animals are fed. It is a concrete location word rather than a description of the food itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs 392 times, so its exact reference can depend on the surrounding sentence. The word appears across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical portions of this Greek corpus, while its central sense remains a place associated with feeding.

word:lxx:L709429.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something carrying wood. It identifies a wood-bearer by the load being carried, giving a straightforward description rather than naming a person, place, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 13:31. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains clear: carrying wood. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation’s language and context.

word:lxx:L709450.explanation: This noun means “journey,” referring to travel from one place to another. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Wisdom and once in 1 Maccabees. Its basic sense is the journey itself rather than a person making the journey or a specific destination. The surrounding wording determines whether the journey is described as ordinary travel or serves a larger purpose in the passage.citep03:word:lxx:L709450:identityp03:word:lxx:L709450:occurrences

word:lxx:L709524.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as pitiable—being in a condition that calls for compassion because of a piteous plight. It focuses on the condition of the person or situation, rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times: once in Jeremiah and three times in deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L709612.explanation: This word refers to a pledge or surety—a person or arrangement that guarantees an agreement and helps preserve unity between parties. As a noun, it names the guarantee itself or the one who stands as security; as an adjective, it can describe something serving that purpose. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs eight times, chiefly in 1 Maccabees and once in Isaiah. Its central idea is dependable assurance that a relationship or agreement will hold together.

word:lxx:L709771.explanation: Orophos refers to reeds used for thatching houses.

word:lxx:L709825.explanation: Ouiechōa, also rendered Oiekhoa, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it functions as an individual name. This name appears once in the Greek LXX, at Ezra 10:36. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the event. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L709898.explanation: This verb means “do” or “go,” describing an action or movement. Depending on the sentence, it can point to carrying something out or to going somewhere. It functions as a verb, so it expresses what someone does or where someone goes rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it is attested once, at Sirach 36:27. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine whether doing or going is intended there.

word:lxx:L709920.explanation: This noun means “paean” or “battle cry”: a voiced expression used as a rallying cry. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 15:25. The definition presents the word as naming the cry itself, rather than an action or person. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise force in that passage cannot be stated more narrowly without adding information beyond the word’s established meaning.

word:lxx:L709959.explanation: This adjective describes something belonging to or involving the "whole community," making it "public" rather than private. It points to what is shared openly by the people as a group. In the Greek LXX, the word appears once, in 2 Maccabees 3:18. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning focuses on the entire community and what is publicly known or experienced.

word:lxx:L710197.explanation: Patroklos is a proper name—the personal name of an individual. It does not describe a general quality, action, or object, but identifies someone specifically. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this name occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be explained further. Its central meaning remains the individual name “Patroklos.”

word:lxx:L710232.explanation: This adverb means “near” or “hard by,” describing something located close to another person or place. It expresses nearness rather than distance and normally answers the question of where something is in relation to something else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 34:2. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains simple: something is close at hand or nearby.

word:lxx:L710294.explanation: This verb means “drape” or “clothe,” describing the act of putting clothing or a covering around someone or something. It functions as an action word, so it focuses on what is being done rather than naming a garment or person. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 69 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing regular use for clothing or covering. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains placing something around or upon another.

word:lxx:L710311.explanation: “Grasping” describes someone or something marked by a grasping quality or character. As an adjective, the word characterizes a person or thing rather than naming an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 1:20. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what the adjective describes there, but its basic lexical idea is grasping.

word:lxx:L710485.explanation: This verb means to make something credible or to confirm another person’s query. It describes giving assurance that a question, request, or claim can be trusted or accepted. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 18:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its basic sense is to establish credibility or confirm what someone has asked.

word:lxx:L710504.explanation: This noun means “scale of a balance,” the weighing instrument used to compare or measure weight. It names a physical tool rather than an action or quality. In this LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense is therefore a tool used for weighing, while the precise force of either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse.

word:lxx:L710636.explanation: This noun means “great experience,” referring to deep or extensive experience gained through what a person has encountered. It describes experience as substantial rather than slight or ordinary. In the Greek Old Testament writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is a wealth of experience.

word:lxx:L710643.explanation: Polyplokos means much-tangled or thick-wreathed, describing varied and subtle artifices.

word:lxx:L710715.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as gentle—marked by a mild, considerate quality rather than forcefulness. It presents gentleness as a recognizable character or manner, though the precise emphasis depends on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:12. Its central meaning remains straightforward: it identifies what is gentle.

word:lxx:L710962.explanation: Prostassō means to order or command.

word:lxx:L711068.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “fold,” referring to something bent over or arranged in a doubled layer. It names the fold itself rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, in Job 41:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains a fold or layered part of something.

word:lxx:L711183.explanation: This word means “slap,” referring to a blow delivered with the hand. It is a noun, so it names the physical act or its result rather than describing an action as a verb. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 50:6. The word itself expresses a direct, physical strike; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand its particular significance there.

word:lxx:L711244.explanation: This verb describes something breaking or bursting open with force. It points to a sudden rupture or the act of giving way, rather than a quiet movement. As a verb, it names an action in which something breaks or bursts, rather than describing an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament, the LXX, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 13:13. Its central meaning is “break; burst,” while the surrounding passage determines exactly what is affected.

word:lxx:L711309.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “rescue”: to deliver someone from danger, trouble, or a destructive situation. It describes an act of saving rather than merely offering help or protection. The word appears 175 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it is a well-established term for deliverance across many settings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on who is being rescued and from what circumstance, but its central idea remains being brought safely out of peril.

word:lxx:L711420.explanation: This noun describes swaying or rocking—the movement of something that shifts back and forth. It presents motion rather than a person, object, or action of speech. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs seven times, appearing in Psalms, Lamentations, Jonah, and Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being described and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains unsteady back-and-forth movement. The word is preserved in passages ranging from the Psalms to later wisdom literature.

word:lxx:L711459.explanation: Samegar is a proper name, referring to a particular person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered as “Samegar” and does not function as a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Judges: Judges 3:31 and Judges 5:6. The name’s precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its basic lexical meaning is simply the personal name Samegar.

word:lxx:L711525.explanation: Sardion means ruby, a precious stone.

word:lxx:L711598.explanation: Se means you, referring to the person being addressed.

word:lxx:L711613.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered as “Sebōin” or “Sevin.” It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Isaiah 45:14. The name’s precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic function is simply to identify the named entity associated with that occurrence.

word:lxx:L711824.explanation: This verb means “ensnare”: to catch, trap, or draw someone into a harmful situation. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so it presents entanglement as something done to someone. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains that of being caught or trapped rather than simply encountering difficulty.

word:lxx:L711929.explanation: This word is the proper name Solomon, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is the Greek LXX form of the name and is rendered “Solomon.” Within the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 8:7. Since no verse text is provided, the word itself establishes the person’s name, while the surrounding passage supplies the specific role or significance of Solomon in that occurrence.

word:lxx:L711950.explanation: Soubal, also rendered Suval, is a personal name rather than a descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies an individual in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles. The name occurs twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles 4:1 and 4:2. Since no further lexical definition or verse text is provided, its meaning is best understood as the identity of the person named, not as a quality, action, or instruction.

word:lxx:L712029.explanation: This adjective describes something connected with a grain field or something sown. It points to land prepared for growing grain, or to seed that has been planted. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Genesis 1:29, and its recorded rendering is “sown.” The word therefore belongs to the language of cultivated provision and planting, while the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the field itself or what has been placed in it.

word:lxx:L712124.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “equipment,” referring broadly to the gear or supplies prepared for use. It is a practical word for the material things needed to outfit a person, group, or undertaking, rather than an abstract quality or action. Within the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 1–3 Maccabees. The exact force in any one passage depends on what kind of equipment the surrounding verse identifies, but the central idea remains prepared gear or supplies.

word:lxx:L712212.explanation: This verb means to “commingle” or “compose”: to mix things together so that they form a combined whole. It can describe elements being blended rather than remaining separate. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs twice, once in Daniel and once in 2 Maccabees. The basic idea is joining or combining parts, while the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

word:lxx:L712371.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “sweep away.” It describes removing or carrying something off by sweeping, rather than merely noticing or moving it. In the Greek Old Testament material represented here, it occurs three times, all in Jeremiah, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word functions as a verb, naming the action itself. Its exact force in each passage is determined by what is being swept away and the sentence around it.

word:lxx:L712490.explanation: This Greek Old Testament noun means “caravan,” referring to a group of travelers journeying together. It describes a traveling company rather than one individual, so the word naturally points to people moving as an organized group. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, all within Nehemiah 7, appearing in two verses: Nehemiah 7:5 and 7:64. Its basic meaning remains straightforward; the surrounding verse determines what people or group the caravan includes in each instance.

word:lxx:L712542.explanation: This verb means “sew”: to join material by stitching it together. It describes a practical action involving fabric or another material that can be sewn, rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears two times, once in Job and once in Ezekiel. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary meaning remains the act of sewing or stitching material together.

word:lxx:L712616.explanation: This word means “school” or “leisure”. As a noun, it can name a place or setting connected with learning, or free time set apart from ordinary work and duties. The central idea is time made available—either for instruction or for rest and personal pursuits. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Genesis, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

word:lxx:L712663.explanation: Sōphan, also rendered “Sofan,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 26:43. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity and role cannot be explained further, but its basic lexical function is clear: it is a personal name.

word:lxx:L712968.explanation: Tritos means third, marking something as number three in an order.

word:lxx:L713057.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “healthy,” describing someone or something as being in a sound, well condition. It expresses the state of health rather than naming a person, object, or place.
